procedure.method: Fresh independent review in this session, with no spawn, fork, resume or peer review. Read the pinned packet, case, rules, rubric, addendum and all five pinned native-evidence manifests; did not follow their unlisted embedded paths. The packet declares no source assets or protected layouts, so the corresponding receipts are explicitly empty. Opened and visually inspected each exact poster with tools.view_image(detail='original'), forwarding the returned image at original detail, in member order M1, M2, M3, M4, M5 and, within each, native then usage720 then thumbnail320. All fifteen opens completed before the first actual copy-reading/transcription stage, any judgment or score. Native views were 1672×941 for M1/M2 and 1024×1536 for M3/M4/M5; usage views were 720×405 and 720×1080 respectively; thumbnails were 320×180 and 213×320. Hash/byte and PNG-header checks corroborated the bindings and sizes but are not substituted for the actual visual opens. First readings used the already displayed native/usage pixels after the full opening sequence; no ambiguity-triggered revisit was needed. No source identity, omitted copy, maker intent, event or runtime session ID was inferred. The seven ratings and whole-set comparison below are my own pixel-based judgments.

thumbnail320
paving diagonals and right-hand glass

The curb and shadows remain scene-defining at small size. The photograph occupies the composition rather than serving as a small ornament on a solid headline field. Its natural depth and public street reflections distinguish it from M2's graphic marks, M3's drawn wear, M4's painted night and M5's harsh printed surface.
native
right two-thirds and foreground

Glass reflects people, vehicles and a lit tree above a large stone sill; textured pavement and long shadows fill the foreground. These nonglyph elements carry the discovery of light and human traces along an ordinary street.

The street's doubled reflection and diagonal light/shadow route are readable and occupy most of the poster, making attentive walking specific rather than relying on the title alone.

The reflected walkers and cars, direct pavement and long light bands reward looking at an ordinary route from more than one angle; the nonglyph scene closely supports finding new stories in familiar surroundings.

upper-left title
The title remains the first readable typographic element; the scene still holds the other half of attention.
native
title and four body lines
The Korean title has coherent serif stroke modulation and open counters; body glyphs, commas, periods and word gaps are intact.
usage720

The full body is easy to continue reading at this width, with consistent leading and no visible shadow crossing that destroys a word.
usage720
left text inset and diagonal sill
The repeated left inset and compact copy block are balanced by the long, receding stone sill. The large pavement foreground is active with directed shadows rather than an unexplained blank.
native
stone sill, metal frame and glass
Pebbled stone, smooth metal and transparent reflections have distinct surface responses to the same warm light; the scene remains coherent despite shallow focus in the distant street.
usage720

Warm light and low pavement viewpoint create a welcoming, observant pause; the public street remains present without dominating the quiet surface study.
native

Frames and paving recede consistently, and the reflection belongs to the glass. No arbitrary decorative marks or clearly contradictory foreground construction are visible; distant figures are softened by depth of field rather than resolved portraits.

residuals: The warm street photograph and conventional title/body setting are professionally coherent, but do not establish exceptional typographic or editorial invention.
Distant reflected figures and storefront detail are optically soft; no exact identity or unreadable sign copy is inferred.
Native 1672×941 is accepted as 16:9 by nearest-integer single-edge rounding: ideal height at width 1672 is 940.5, a 0.5 px difference. It is not mathematically exact 16:9.

evidence: thumbnail320
street panorama and mirrored glass

The warm photographic public street, deep reflections and long pavement shadows give M1 an observational daylight identity. Compared with M3's tight drawn threshold, it uses believable street depth and actual-looking reflected activity rather than isolated wear.
thumbnail320
yellow/navy perspective and red prints

M2's saturated planar contrast, monumental gothic line and distressed sole route form the most outward and graphic identity. Its simplified light/shadow geometry and walking marks differ in construction, emotional energy and type voice from all four surface scenes.
usage720
pale cracked wall, door handle and step

M3's fine contour drawing, light washes, blue/cream relationship and serif body create quiet close observation of use and age. It shares a legible upper-left reading order with M1/M4, but its object intimacy, surface drawing and daylight restraint are distinct from their photographic public depth and painted night warmth.
thumbnail320
dark wall, lit window and golden pavement

M4's heavy brush marks, cool-dark/amber relationship and luminous occupied window give an intimate nocturnal identity. The emotional center is interior life reflecting outward, unlike M3's weathered threshold or M5's abrasive infrastructure; its similar two-line title layout does not erase that difference.
usage720
overhead drain, rough print and diagonal cream band

M5 has hard printed value separation, coarse teal/cream/black surface, a downward crop and heavier one-line serif anchor. Compared with M3, the object, viewing angle, tonal force, glyph weight and emotional abrasion change together; this is more than adding a filter to the same doorway composition.
residuals: All five use a left-aligned title followed immediately by a four-line body; M1/M3/M4 also have closely related serif headline voices. This shared functional order is allowed, but limits the set's typographic breadth.

M1/M3/M4/M5 all study street surfaces or building edges. Their differing scene relationships, image construction, light/contrast and emotional effects achieve five recognizable identities, while the common observational family keeps diversity at 4 rather than exceptional 5.
The five members and this single editorial review are fully assessed. No claim is made about the two other critics, their scores, the all-three gate or unseen requests.
